data.title: Middle East Eye: Britain's definition of 'anti-Muslim hostility' protects the state, not those being targeted
data.author: Karsen Trull
data.summary:
Britain's definition of 'anti-Muslim hostility' protects the state, not those being targeted
Submitted by
Karsen Trull
on
Thu, 11/12/2026 - 14:09
New report from Cage International shows how UK policy leaves the central mechanism of post-9/11 Islamophobia untouched - and lends it official cover
Britain's definition of anti-Muslim hostility 'is not a failed attempt to protect Muslims. It is a successful attempt to protect the state' (Reuters)
Off
This year marked a quarter of a century since the beginning of the “war on terror”, and in that time, the British state has built one of the most extensive counter-extremism systems in the world.
Also this year, Britain produced - for the first time - an official definition of what it calls “anti-Muslim hostility”. It would be easy to treat these as separate stories, one about security and the other about community relations - but a new report from Cage International argues that they are not.
The definition has been shaped so precisely around the security state that, read closely, it functions less as a protection for Muslims than as a protection for the institutions that have spent two decades treating them as suspects.
The key, as the report sets out, lies in a single word that runs through every part of the definition: intent. Anti-Muslim hostility, as the government defines it, means intentionally engaging in criminal acts against Muslims, or stereotyping them “with the intention of encouraging hatred.” It means discrimination where the conduct “is intended to disadvantage Muslims in public and economic life”.
Discrimination rarely announces itself this way. The Islamophobia Response Unit, a charity that handles discrimination casework, has warned that the threshold excludes most of the cases it sees: bias, institutional barriers, and recruitment processes that quietly filter out applicants with Muslim names.

Andreas Malm attends the "How To Blow Up A Pipeline" premiere during the 2022 Toronto International Film Festival on 10 September 2022 in Toronto, Ontario (Jeremy Chan/Getty Images/AFP )
Off
The UK Home Office pushed Hackney Council to cancel an event featuring Swedish climate scholar Andreas Malm and Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori, despite the Home Office's own assessment which found the event "did not meet the threshold for disruption," disclosures suggest.
In October, Malm was barred from entering the UK by the Home Office, and instead was set to appear by video link at the event for the magazine Tribune on 4 November at a venue owned by Hackney Council.
The event coincided with a legal challenge against the UK government’s controversial ban against Palestine Action which Ammori is fighting in the Supreme Court.
Freedom of Information and Subject Access Request documents released to Tribune appear to show that in the run-up to the event, the Home Office tried to pressure Hackney Council officials into cancelling it by warning them that it could breach the Terrorism Act 2000 due to Ammori’s participation.
The disclosures reveal that an initial Home Office assessment found that the event was “unlikely to meet the threshold for disruption”.
Despite this, the Home Office contacted the Prevent and Hate Crime coordinator of Hackney Council, warning them that the event would feature “two speakers of concern” and sharing with them an intelligence summary used to bar Malm from entering the UK, which described him “legitimis[ing] and encoura[ing] attacks on energy infrastructure and terrorism”.

The decision, signalled in an order first reported by MEE in August, raises questions over whether the court is seeking to ease US pressure following sanctions
Rosario Salvatore Aitala, now presiding judge of the ICC’s Pre-Trial Chamber II, at his swearing-in ceremony in The Hague on 9 March 2018 (ICC/Flikr)
Off
Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) have ordered the closure of the court’s Afghanistan investigation that covered alleged war crimes by US forces, despite ongoing attempts by prosecutors to appeal the decision.
Ending the investigation into alleged US crimes addresses one of Washington’s longstanding objections to the ICC and one of the reasons behind the sanctions on the court and its officials.
The move is therefore likely to raise questions about whether the court is seeking to ease tensions with Washington by signalling that it will no longer pursue allegations against US forces and their allies.
The Afghanistan situation at the ICC dates back to November 2017, when then-prosecutor Fatou Bensouda first requested authorisation to investigate alleged crimes committed since 2003, including by Afghan and US forces as well as the Taliban and the IS-K group.
That request was initially rejected by a differently composed pre-trial chamber in 2019, before the appeals chamber overturned the decision in March 2020 and authorised the investigation to proceed.
Bensouda was sanctioned by the US government a few months later over alleged attempts to subject Americans to the court's jurisdiction. Members of the appeals chamber that authorised the decision were also later sanctioned.

The UK parliament’s standards commissioner has been urged to investigate the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Israel following reports linking its funding to an Israeli organisation that says it helps shape debate in the British parliament.
The APPG is funded by Cedarsoak Ltd, a British company in which Lord Mendelsohn, the former chair of Labour Friends of Israel, and Lord Polak, the former director of the Conservative Friends of Israel, are the sole directors.
But Byline Times reported earlier this month that the Tel Aviv-based firm Cedars Oak Israel Ltd owed the UK firm Cedarsoak £147,687 in reimbursements in 2024.
Cedars Oak Israel describes itself as taking "an active part in shaping the narrative in the British Parliament" to "serve national objectives".
Its 2024 report to the Israeli charity registrar said it worked to influence British opinion and policy on Hamas, antisemitism, sanctions, Iran and other issues.
The firm's donor in 2024 was Line Trust Corporation Limited, a Gibraltar-based trust company owned by Hassans, the territory's biggest law firm.
APPGs, which are informal groups of MPs and peers, are required to name any party that "ultimately funded" a benefit according to parliamentary rules.
According to Byline Times, the APPG also retroactively registered a benefit-in-kind, valued at between £85,501 and £87,000, from Cedarsoak Ltd in early 2025.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Saudi-backed forces retreat from Bab al-Mandab as Houthis gain ground
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:

Submitted by

on

The Southern Armed Forces say the move is intended to reinforce Aden, while the Houthis claim they drove troops from positions overlooking the strategic waterway
Supporters of Yemen’s Houthi authorities gather during a protest against Saudi intervention in Sanaa, 9 October 2026 (Mohammed Huwais/AFP)
Off
Saudi-backed forces in Yemen have withdrawn from positions overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving the Houthis with greater leverage over the southern entrance to the Red Sea after weeks of fighting.
The Southern Armed Forces, who are backed by Saudi Arabia and fighting alongside the internationally recognised Yemeni government, said on Sunday they had "redeployed" troops from Dhubab airport and surrounding regions of Bab al-Mandab to strengthen defences around the interim capital Aden.
“This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats,” the group said in a statement.
The Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, offered a different account. A military source quoted by the Houthi-run Saba news agency said that they had forced Saudi-backed forces out of positions around Dhubab and Bab al-Mandab after severing their rear supply routes, forcing them to move towards Aden.

Bilal Erdogan, the Turkish president’s son, also made a three-day trip to Lebanon last week, meeting officials, dignitaries and community leaders.
Several Ankara insiders told Middle East Eye that Turkey was seeking to deepen its ties across the Levant, particularly following the rise of a new Syrian government in Damascus. That transition has allowed Turkish officials to encourage dialogue between Syria and Lebanon.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani visited Beirut in July, in a trip described as opening a new chapter in relations between the two countries.
Ankara believes stability in Syria can be achieved only if Lebanon is also stable.

Palestinian lawmaker Ahmad Tibi was appointed temporary deputy speaker of Israel's parliament on Monday, securing a prominent position after parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel made significant gains in last month's election.
The Times of Israel reported that the Knesset's Arrangements Committee approved a list of nine temporary deputy speakers by 13-9 votes following a heated debate.
It said the the approved deputy speakers were Tibi, who chairs the Joint List alliance and leads the Ta'al party, United Arab List (Ra'am) MP Walid Taha, B'Yachad MP Eitan Ginzburg, Democrats MP Yair Fink, Yisrael Beytenu MP Oded Forer, United Torah Judaism MP Yitzhak Pindrus, Likud MP Yaakov Bardugo, Otzma Yehudit MP Limor Son Har-Melech and Shas MP Michael Malkieli.
According to the Times of Israel, the temporary deputies will serve until permanent deputy Knesset speakers are appointed.
It also reported that the during the debate, Likud MP Ofir Katz accused the committee of "normalising terror supporters," while Otzma Yehudit MP Yitzhak Kroizer called the appointments a "Rubicon that must not be crossed."
Speaking to Al Jazeera after the vote, Tibi said that his appointment was a "rightful achievement" for the alliance, which secured 11 seats in the 27 October election.
The Joint List and Ra'am, which represent Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a combined 19 seats in the 120-member parliament, marking a significant increase in their representation.
